description: We are a group of university students from diverse academic backgrounds, with one member studying Environmental Science, another Computer Science, and the third Artificial Intelligence. Despite our different areas of study, we share a common interest in spatial data and its applications.
summary:
Climate change makes agricultural planning increasingly uncertain, especially for farmers in lower-income countries who depend on rain-fed agriculture. Understanding historical climate patterns and anticipating future changes can help farmers make more informed decisions. However, complex scientific datasets may be difficult to interpret without specialised knowledge.

Our project, Vanni the Farmer, addresses this through an interactive climate exploration tool that makes climate information more accessible to farmers. Using multiple NASA climate datasets, including GLDAS Noah 2.1, MERRA-2 and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, we examine historical precipitation, soil moisture, air temperature and land evapotranspiration, alongside future temperature and precipitation projections. Together, these variables help characterise local climate conditions.

Through statistical analysis and visualisation, farmers can examine seasonal patterns, identify long-term trends, compare environmental conditions across years and detect unusual patterns or significant differences between periods. These insights can help farmers understand how temperature and rainfall patterns are changing in their regions, allowing them to anticipate potential changes in water availability and temperature conditions that may affect agricultural activities. Ultimately, Vanni the Farmer aims to support farmers in making more informed agricultural decisions and strengthen their capacity to anticipate and adapt to climate change.
details:
Project Overview

  • Vanni the Farmer is an interactive climate exploration tool designed to help farmers investigate historical environmental trends and explore potential future climate conditions in their geographical regions. The platform consists of two main components, Historical Trend Analysis and Future Climate Scenarios, which allow users to examine past environmental changes and explore possible future climate conditions.
  • Users can select their area of interest by placing a point on the map, drawing a boundary or entering a location in the search bar.

Historical Trend Analysis 

  • Purpose: Allows users to examine changes in six environmental variables: total surface precipitation, surface soil moisture (0–10 cm), 2-metre air temperature, total land evapotranspiration, minimum temperature and maximum temperature.
  • User inputs: Environmental variables, time period and data frequency (daily, monthly or yearly).
  • Visualisation and analysis: Generates time-series graphs to visualise changes in environmental conditions over time. Anomaly analysis is conducted to identify periods when environmental conditions deviate from historical averages. Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope are applied to yearly data to assess the direction, magnitude and statistical significance of historical trends. 

Future Climate Scenarios

  • Purpose: Allows users to explore potential changes in five environmental variables: precipitation, minimum temperature, maximum temperature, wettest day of the year and days above 35°C under different future climate scenarios.
  • User inputs: Environmental variables, future time periods and Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios.
  • Visualisation and analysis: Generates interactive time-series graphs to visualise projected changes in environmental conditions and compare the two emissions scenarios. Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope are applied to assess the direction, magnitude and statistical significance of projected climate trends. Mann-Whitney U test is used to compare environmental conditions between the two emissions scenarios over the same time period and assess whether differences are statistically significant.

Innovation 

  • Makes climate data more accessible to farmers by presenting complex datasets and statistical analyses through an interactive interface, time-series graphs and straightforward statistical summaries.
  • Provides location-specific climate exploration, allowing users to examine environmental conditions relevant to their agricultural areas without manually entering geographical coordinates.
  • Integrates historical climate analysis and future climate projections within a single platform, reducing the need to navigate multiple climate data sources.

Design considerations 

  • Location flexibility: Designed to accommodate different geographical areas and user needs by allowing users to choose their selected locations, environmental variables and time periods.
  • Selection of relevant climate variables: Prioritises variables that provide insights into agricultural conditions, particularly water availability, rainfall patterns and temperature conditions.
  • Interpretation of climate trends and uncertainty: Incorporates statistical tests and anomaly analysis to distinguish longer-term trends from short-term fluctuations. Two contrasting emissions scenarios are also included to illustrate the range of possible future climate conditions.
  • Data visualisation: Uses time-series graphs and statistical summaries to present climate information in a format that is easier to interpret than raw datasets.
  • Data accessibility and performance: Uses pre-processed climate datasets for Southeast Asia and South Asia to improve data accessibility and reduce retrieval and processing demands, while allowing users to explore other regions through NASA's publicly available climate datasets 

Intended impacts

  • Supports current agricultural decision-making by helping farmers identify long-term climate patterns in their selected areas. For example, historical rainfall trends can provide insights into changes in water availability in the land, while temperature trends can help inform decisions on crop selection, planting schedules and water management.
  • Supports longer-term adaptation by helping farmers anticipate how changing climate conditions could affect their agricultural areas. For instance, projected increases in temperature or changes in precipitation could help farmers consider adjustments to crop varieties, planting schedules and irrigation practices to better prepare for future climate conditions.

Tools & Technologies used

Data and datasets

  • Historical datasets: NASA GPM IMERG (precipitation), GLDAS Noah 2.1 (soil moisture and evapotranspiration) and MERRA-2 (temperature), accessed through NASA Giovanni via the Harmony API 
  • Future climate projections: NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 dataset, using the GFDL-ESM4 climate model and two emissions scenarios, SSP1-2.6 (low-emissions, best-case scenario) and SSP5-8.5 (very high-emissions, worst-case scenario). A pre-processed dataset was prepared for Southeast Asia and South Asia, while data for other regions are retrieved from NASA's public AWS S3 bucket and NCCS THREDDS server
  • Data format: NetCDF

Computational environment and storage

  • Language: Python
  • Environment: Google Colab for computational work.
  • Storage: Google Drive for persistent data storage.

Backend development

  • Language and framework: Python 3.12 and FastAPI.
  • Data retrieval: NASA Harmony API and NASA Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for accessing and identifying historical datasets.
  • Authentication and hosting: NASA Earthdata Login for data access authentication, with the token stored as an environment secret on Render. The backend is hosted on Render.
  • Climate projection API: climateprojectionsAPI, developed using FastAPI to serve future climate projection outputs.
  • Python libraries: Pandas, NumPy, xarray and netCDF4 for data handling and numerical operations, SciPy for statistical analyses, including linear regression, Theil-Sen estimation and Mann-Whitney U tests, Shapely for geographical and boundary-related spatial operations, pytest for software testing

Frontend development

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Mapping and location APIs: Google Maps API for geographical selection, Google Geocoding API and OpenStreetMap Nominatim for location searches, and the browser's Geolocation API for automatic location detection.
  • Data visualisation: Chart.js 4 for generating interactive graphs and visualising climate trends and projections.
